name: Posterior cruciate ligament
description: Intra-articular, extrasynovial ligament from the lateral surface of the medial femoral condyle in the anterior notch to the posterior intercondylar area (PCL facet) of the tibia below the joint line, with a larger anterolateral and a smaller posteromedial bundle. It is about 32–38 mm long with roughly 1.2–2 times the cross-sectional area of the ACL. It is uniformly low in signal on all sequences and unstriated, forming a smooth, gentle arc on sagittal images in near extension, and is usually seen whole on one sagittal slice.

normal_values.ap_diameter_vertical_portion: under 7 mm on sagittal T2, across the mid vertical segment; 7 mm or more strongly suggests a tear (Rodriguez 2008)
normal_values.pcl_angle: sagittal angle between the proximal and distal limbs; below 107° (Gentili 1994) to below 115° (Mellado 2004) supports an ACL tear (specificity 82–94%, sensitivity 52–70%)

variants_pitfalls: Magic angle: the proximal curve, where fibers lie near 55° to B0, can show intermediate signal on short-TE images (PD, T1, GRE) that fades on long-TE T2. Tears can also be brighter on PD than T2 (Rodriguez 2008), so let thickness (7 mm or more), fiber continuity and periligamentous edema decide, not signal alone.

Buckled PCL: an exaggerated, question-mark curve (PCL angle below about 107–115°) reflects anterior tibial translation and is an indirect sign of ACL tear; it can also appear with hyperextension in a knee with an intact ACL (Nissman 2008), so confirm on the ACL itself.

Meniscofemoral ligaments: at least one in about 93% of knees (cadaver, Gupte 2002: Humphry 74%, Wrisberg 69%; 93 of 100 MRIs, Cho 1999), with Wrisberg (posterior to the PCL) seen far more often than Humphry (anterior) on MRI. Either can mimic a loose body, focal PCL thickening or a partial tear; trace it from the lateral meniscus posterior horn to the medial femoral condyle.

Double PCL sign: a second low-signal band parallel to the PCL, just anteroinferior to it and running along much of its length, is a displaced bucket-handle fragment, almost always of the medial meniscus. A ligament of Humphry lies in the same place but is thin (about 1.5–2 mm, about 8% of the PCL cross-section) and can be traced to the lateral meniscus posterior horn; confirm a fragment with an absent bow tie and a truncated meniscal body on coronal and sagittal images.

PCL tears usually stay in continuity: a thickened PCL with intermediate intrasubstance signal is the common look of an interstitial tear, and chronic tears can heal lax and elongated, looking near normal. A fibular styloid avulsion (arcuate sign) should prompt a close look; all 13 patients in Huang 2003 had a PCL injury.
